contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Use pair search when pointer movement eliminates classes of endpoint pairs; use a running window when advancing the right boundary reuses state for contiguous candidates and the left boundary repairs validity.

authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring; human review required

items.prompt: In a sorted array, compare a[left] + a[right] with T. If the sum is too small, increment left; if it is too large, decrement right. No aggregate for the interior is stored. What search model is being used?

options.text: Use a two-pointers invariant.
Use a sliding-window validity invariant.
Classify it as two pointers solely because two indices appear.

feedback.reason: Each comparison eliminates a class of endpoint pairs; there is no running contiguous candidate.

blocks.text: The state is the current pair of endpoints. Sorted order proves that a too-small sum cannot be fixed by keeping the smaller endpoint and choosing an even smaller partner, while a too-large sum cannot be fixed by keeping the larger endpoint and choosing an even larger partner. This is global pair-space elimination. A sliding window would instead carry forward state for [left, right] as right advances and would move left to repair a validity predicate for that range. The absence of an interior aggregate is not merely an implementation detail; it reflects a different candidate space.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sliding_window: The endpoints enclose values, but the algorithm neither treats them as one candidate nor maintains range state. Movement eliminates endpoint pairs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.indices_only: Two indices describe the implementation, while sorted endpoint elimination supplies the actual classification.

constraints: Input is sorted in nondecreasing order.
Only endpoint values are compared.

items.prompt: To find the longest substring containing at most K distinct characters, right advances one character at a time, a frequency map is updated, and left advances only until the current substring is valid again. Which model explains the linear scan?

options.text: Use a two-pointers invariant.
Use a sliding-window validity invariant.
Classify it as two pointers solely because two indices appear.

feedback.reason: Each right step reuses and repairs state for the current contiguous substring.

blocks.text: The algorithm does not restart a search for every pair of indices. It carries a frequency map from one right endpoint to the next, adding the entering character and removing characters that leave from the left. That reuse is the running-window mechanism: candidates ending at successive right positions share almost all of their contents. The at-most-K predicate is also repairable by shrinking because removing characters cannot introduce a new distinct character. A global pair search would compare isolated endpoint relations rather than maintain the membership state of every character inside the range.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_pointers: Although two indices move, the decisive state is the frequency map for all characters in the current range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.indices_only: The variable count cannot explain why the algorithm is linear. Reused range state and validity repair do.

constraints: The candidate must be a contiguous substring.
K is a nonnegative integer fixed for the task.

items.prompt: Which statement most directly distinguishes a global pair search from a running window?

options.text: Pair search uses an endpoint comparison to eliminate impossible endpoint combinations; a window reuses state for a contiguous candidate and removes starts under a validity rule.
Pair search always moves inward, while a window always moves both indices to the right.
Pair search has two index variables, while a window has more than two state variables.
Pair search requires sorted input, while a window never uses sorted input.

feedback.reason: The decisive distinction is how the algorithm reuses or eliminates candidate space, not pointer direction or variable count.

blocks.text: Both families can use same-direction pointers, and either may carry auxiliary state. What matters is the justification for not reconsidering candidates. In pair search, an endpoint relation—often supported by ordering—rules out a set of pairs. In a running window, the algorithm reuses state for contiguous candidates and advances left because earlier starts are invalid or dominated under the window rule. This proof-level distinction transfers to unfamiliar code more reliably than surface rules about direction, sorting, or the number of variables.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.direction_only: This is a common mnemonic but not a contract. Same-direction read/write two pointers exist, and some windows can have fixed width.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_variables: Both families commonly use two indices and may use additional state. Variable count does not identify the candidate space.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_only: Sortedness often supports pair elimination, but it is neither required by every two-pointers problem nor forbidden for windows.

constraints: Assume either candidate may use two indices and auxiliary state; classify by candidate-space reasoning.

items.prompt: A sorted sequence is scanned from both ends to find the pair with sum closest to T. Each step evaluates only the two endpoint values and moves one endpoint according to whether the sum is below or above T. Is the shrinking span a sliding window?

options.text: No. The span is the unresolved domain of endpoint pairs, not a maintained contiguous candidate.
Yes. Any pair of boundaries that moves inward is a window.
Yes. The distance right - left changes on every step.

feedback.reason: The enclosed span is search space, while the actual candidate is the endpoint pair.

blocks.text: A visual interval can represent different semantics. Here the algorithm does not score or validate every element in the interval. It uses the endpoints to form one pair and relies on order to choose which class of pairs can be discarded. Calling the unresolved domain a window would obscure the proof: no entering/leaving aggregate is maintained and no range-validity predicate is repaired. A changing width or inward motion is therefore insufficient evidence for sliding window.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_shrinking_window: Boundary motion alone is not a window invariant. The interior values are not maintained as one candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_length_changes: Changing interval length is a visual property, not the algorithm's candidate or proof obligation.

constraints: Only endpoint values contribute to each evaluated candidate.

items.prompt: An original task asks whether two sorted values differ by exactly D. A revised task asks for the longest contiguous segment whose maximum minus minimum is at most D, and supplies data structures that maintain the segment extrema as right advances. Which structural change requires a running-window model?

options.text: The revised candidate is a contiguous segment whose maintained extrema are reused across successive right endpoints.
Both tasks compare a quantity with D.
Both implementations may use left and right.
The word longest appears in the revised task.

feedback.reason: The revised task introduces a reusable contiguous candidate with state owned by the entire range.

blocks.text: The threshold D is shared, but the candidate space is not. The original task evaluates a relation between two selected values. The revised task evaluates every member of a contiguous segment through its extrema and reuses that state as the segment expands and shrinks. The word “longest” alone is not decisive; longest-pair-distance problems still exist. The decisive change is that the answer and validity belong to a running interval, allowing successive candidates to share maintained state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_threshold: Sharing a numeric threshold does not preserve the same candidate space or invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_boundaries: Both patterns can use these variables. The revised range state, not the names, drives the change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.optimization_word: Optimization wording is not enough; the relevant fact is that the entire contiguous segment is maintained.

constraints: The revised segment must preserve original-order contiguity.
The maintained extrema represent all elements currently in the segment.
D is nonnegative.

items.prompt: A problem asks for any two positions with difference at most D; all positions between them are irrelevant. Why is a running window aggregate not the default model?

options.text: The candidate is the selected pair, so movement should be justified by the relation between its endpoints rather than by state for the enclosed range.
Any numerical span between indices is a window whose interior must be tracked.
A difference relation always requires maintaining the sum of all interior values.
Sort positions by value so the pair becomes a window automatically.

feedback.reason: The output contract selects two positions and does not make the enclosed values part of the candidate state.

blocks.text: A window is not defined by geometric enclosure alone. It owns a contiguous range and maintains whatever aggregate or membership predicate the whole range requires. Here the only tested relation is between two selected values or positions, so interior values can be ignored. A pair-search proof should explain which endpoint moves and why, independently of any window sum or frequency state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_by_span: A span may be bounded by two indices without its interior being semantically selected.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_required: The problem defines a difference relation on endpoints, not an interior sum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_for_contiguity: Sorting changes positions and does not make irrelevant interior values part of the answer.

constraints: Only the two chosen positions and their difference are evaluated.

items.prompt: A sequence asks for the longest contiguous segment with average at most A, and all values are nonnegative. Which extra state makes it a running-window problem rather than a global pair search?

options.text: Maintain the complete range sum and length; the average predicate depends on every element between left and right.
Compare only the average of the two endpoint values.
Select any two values whose sum is at most 2A; the interior does not matter.
Sort values first so endpoint values represent the range average.

feedback.reason: The predicate is a property of the full contiguous candidate, so its aggregate state must move with the boundaries.

blocks.text: The range average is sum divided by length, and either quantity changes when an interior value enters or leaves. The algorithm therefore owns the entire interval and updates its state as right expands and left shrinks. Endpoint comparisons or pair sums answer different questions and cannot establish the average of all enclosed values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoint_average: The average of endpoints does not determine the average of the interior values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pair_target: A pair sum ignores the values that contribute to the required contiguous segment average.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_values: Sorting destroys original adjacency and does not make endpoints summarize a range average.

constraints: The answer must be a segment of the original sequence.
Values are nonnegative.

items.prompt: Two implementations both update a variable called currentSum when right advances. What evidence distinguishes global pair search from a running window?

options.text: Check whether currentSum represents every value in [left, right] and whether left evicts its contribution; if so, it is a window, not merely a pair scan.
The variable name currentSum proves the algorithm is a window.
Any update when right moves proves that interior values are irrelevant.
The number of indices is enough to classify both implementations.

feedback.reason: A variable's name or one update is not enough; candidate ownership and left-eviction semantics expose the invariant.

blocks.text: A pair algorithm might compute a local expression when a new endpoint is considered, while a window maintains an aggregate for every current member and subtracts values as left advances. The reviewer should ask what currentSum means at every iteration and whether it remains equal to the full range sum. This semantic equality, not the presence of a sum variable, distinguishes the patterns.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_name_decides: Names are arbitrary and may describe a temporary pair calculation rather than range-owned state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_only: A window must also remove left contributions; right updates alone do not define candidate membership.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_indices_decide: Both global pair scans and windows commonly use two boundaries.

constraints: The review must infer semantics from the update invariant, not variable names.

items.prompt: Select all statements that correctly contrast a global pair candidate with a running window candidate.

options.text: A pair candidate can ignore values between its selected positions if the objective refers only to the pair.
A window candidate must include the full interior state needed for its validity or score.
Any movement of left or right uses the same discard proof in both patterns.
Writing [left, right] is sufficient to prove that the candidate is a window.

feedback.reason: Candidate membership and state ownership determine the proof obligations; shared notation does not.

blocks.text: Pair search reasons about two selected positions and uses a relation to discard impossible endpoint choices. A window reasons about one contiguous interval and repairs or extends its complete state. Both may be written with left and right, but the meanings of a pointer move differ. The transfer rule is to identify what remains a live candidate after each update.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_proof: The same pointer direction can implement different invariants and eliminate different sets of candidates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_notation_enough: Notation describes boundaries, not whether interior values are semantically included.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.pair_interior_irrelevant: It identifies when an endpoint relation is sufficient.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.window_interior_material: It identifies when range-owned state is required.

constraints: More than one statement is correct.

items.prompt: A prompt says “find the best interval [left, right]” but never says whether the objective uses only endpoints or all elements inside. What clarification has highest priority?

options.text: Define candidate membership and the state used to score or validate it: selected endpoints only versus the complete contiguous range.
Assume a window because the word interval appears in the prompt.
Assume a pair because only two variables are named.
Choose the pattern that has the expected time complexity before reading the objective.

feedback.reason: The ambiguous output contract determines whether interior elements are candidates and therefore which invariant is legal.

blocks.text: If endpoints alone define the answer, a pair relation may support movement through ordered candidates. If every enclosed element contributes, the algorithm must maintain a range aggregate or membership state and use window updates. “Interval” and two variable names are insufficient. The contract should be clarified before implementation so that the proof and data structure match the intended candidate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.assume_window: A geometric interval may still represent only two selected endpoints; the interior contract is missing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.assume_pair: Two boundaries can own a full range state, so variable count does not select pair search.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.choose_by_complexity: Both patterns can be linear, and complexity cannot compensate for an undefined objective.

constraints: The candidate's interior membership is intentionally unspecified until clarification.

A tree path because endpoints define a range.

blocks.text: Two variables, a loop, or linear complexity can appear in both patterns. The decisive evidence is what the retained state represents and which pointer movement the proof permits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window: Endpoint count does not determine state.
